en: The Chapter on Non-Proliferation, Concerning the Question on Inference.
10. The Question on the Intense Heat of Winter “Venerable Nāgasena, for what reason does the sun shine with such intense heat in winter, and not so in summer?
“In summer, great king, dust and dirt remain undisturbed; the particles stirred up by the wind follow after the sky.”
In the sky, there are thick clouds and a great wind blows excessively;
all these, coming together from various directions, obscure the rays of the sun, and because of that, the sun shines feebly in the summer.
But in the winter, Great King, the earth below is cooled and a great cloud is present above.
Dust and dirt become stilled; the pollen moves about, becoming increasingly still in the sky; the atmosphere becomes free of clouds;
and the wind blows very gently. With the subsiding of these conditions, the sun’s rays become purified, and the heat of the sun, freed from all obstruction, shines with exceeding brilliance.
“This, Great King, is the reason why the sun burns fiercely in the winter, but not so in the summer.
“Venerable sir, the sun burns fiercely when it is free from all distress; it does not burn fiercely when accompanied by clouds and the like.
The tenth inquiry, on the fierce burning of the sun.
In this chapter there are ten questions.
